rows.question: A container is alive, but users should not reach it until its warm-up work is complete. Which Kubernetes mechanism controls that?
rows.answer: To ensure that users do not reach a container until its warm-up work is complete, you should use a Readiness Probe. The Readiness Probe determines when a container is ready to start accepting traffic. Until the Readiness Probe succeeds, the container will not be added to the service endpoints, preventing traffic from reaching it.

rows.question: My application instances get new addresses whenever they are replaced. What gives callers one durable destination?
rows.answer: In Kubernetes, Services provide a stable network endpoint for a set of Pods. When Pods are replaced and their IP addresses change, a Service can be used to expose these Pods over the network with a consistent address. This allows callers to connect to the Service's stable IP address or DNS name, rather than directly to the ephemeral IP addresses of individual Pods. This abstraction ensures that your application instances have a durable destination for network communication.

rows.question: I need every eligible node to run exactly one copy of a log collector. Which controller fits?
rows.answer: To ensure that every eligible node runs exactly one copy of a log collector, you should use a DaemonSet. A DaemonSet ensures that a copy of a Pod runs on all or some nodes, which is ideal for node-level logging where a logging agent must run on every node.

Concepts › Workloads › Controllers › Daemonset Concepts › Workloads › Controllers › Daemonset DaemonSet | Kubernetes DaemonSetA DaemonSet defines Pods that provide node-local facilities. These might be fundamental to the operation of your cluster, such as a networking helper tool, or be part of an add-on.A DaemonSet ensures that all (or some) Nodes run a copy of a Pod. As nodes are added to the cluster, Pods are added to them. As nodes are removed from the cluster, those Pods are garbage collected. Deleting a DaemonSet will clean up the Pods it created.Some typical uses of a DaemonSet are:running a cluster storage daemon on every noderunning a logs collection daemon on every noderunning a node monitoring daemon on every nodeIn a simple case, one DaemonSet, covering all nodes, would be used for each type of daemon. A more complex setup might use multiple DaemonSets for a single type of daemon, but with different flags and/or different memory and cpu requests for different hardware types

rows.question: A batch calculation should run to completion and be retried if its Pod fails. What should own it?
rows.answer: A Kubernetes Job should own the batch calculation task. Jobs are designed to run tasks to completion and will retry execution of the Pods until a specified number of them successfully terminate. This makes them suitable for tasks that need to be retried if a Pod fails.

Concepts › Workloads › Controllers › Job Jobs | Kubernetes JobsJobs represent one-off tasks that run to completion and then stop.A Job creates one or more Pods and will continue to retry execution of the Pods until a specified number of them successfully terminate. As pods successfully complete, the Job tracks the successful completions. When a specified number of successful completions is reached, the task (ie, Job) is complete. Deleting a Job will clean up the Pods it created. Suspending a Job will delete its active Pods until the Job is resumed again.A simple case is to create one Job object in order to reliably run one Pod to completion. The Job object will start a new Pod if the first Pod fails or is deleted (for example due to a node hardware failure or a node reboot).You can also use a Job to run multiple Pods in parallel.If you want to run a Job (either a single task, or several in parallel) on a schedule, see CronJob.Running an example JobHere is an example Job config. rows.ground_truth: A Kubernetes Job should own the workload. A Job creates Pods for a finite task, tracks successful completions, and can retry failed Pods according to its restart and backoff policy.
